Finding warehouse space is rarely as simple as finding an available building.
Saudi Arabia's ambitions in commerce, manufacturing, tourism and logistics are creating new opportunities for businesses across the Kingdom.

An e-commerce company may need inventory positioned near several customer markets. A food supplier may require temperature-controlled storage. A cosmetics distributor may need properly licensed facilities. An industrial company may require space for spare parts or equipment.

At the same time, warehouse operators face a different challenge.

A network-based model can extend geographic coverage without requiring the company to purchase or develop every warehouse in its system.
It can also help warehouse operators gain access to new customer demand while benefiting from shared technology and operating procedures.
Its network extended across more than 120 warehouses and over 60 transportation providers.

Sirdab wants to use AI to improve the matching of customer requirements with suitable logistics capacity and automate parts of the coordination between shippers, warehouse operators and transportation providers.

The same report projected warehouse demand rising from around 87 million square metres in 2023 to approximately 115 million square metres by 2030.
The company is not attempting to reinvent the warehouse building itself.
It is changing the commercial and operational relationship between businesses that need warehouse capacity and providers that can supply it.
More warehouses. More equipment. More facilities. More permanent operating capacity.
Its continued development will depend on the quality of the relationships it builds with warehouse operators, transportation providers and enterprise customers.
Warehouses, transportation networks and inventory systems will remain essential physical infrastructure.
Its biggest opportunity may not be filling more warehouses. It may be helping more businesses grow without the burden of building an entire logistics network themselves.
